newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss cultists gather for sensual meditation.
newsitem.headline: Swiss cultists gather for sensual meditation.

text.p: Members of a bizarre Swiss-based cult that wants to clone humans gathered on Wednesday for a week of sensual meditation and "cosmic orgasm" in the shadow of the Swiss Alps.

Outsiders were not welcome at the gathering of some 500 followers of a Frenchman calling himself Rael, a journalist turned sect leader who says humans were created in laboratories by aliens and claims 35,000 followers in 85 countries.

Young, glamorous Raelians in designer clothes packed into a sports hall in a mountain valley to celebrate their "new year" on the anniversary of the 1945 atomic bombing of Hiroshima, the beginning of their era of "apocalypse".
Journalists were told to leave as lights were dimmed and curtains drawn inside the hall where members including pre-teenage girls listened to pop music and a song about "maple syrup".
Asked what would happen at the party, an Aboriginal member said: "We will sing. Then we will masturbate and sleep. Everyone."
Masturbation, communal orgasm, sexual freedom and pleasure are the main ideas of the movement, whose gathering also confirmed Rael as supreme leader in a Soviet-style election.
Swiss police said they were closely monitoring the movement, which demands unquestioning obedience from its followers.
"We know where they are but our hands are tied unless there is criminality," said local police spokesman Carlo Kuonen.
Rael has set up a firm to offer infertile or gay couples the chance to have a baby cloned from one of his cult's members.

Human cloning is banned in the United States. Many other governments have banned or are preparing to ban cloning research on human embryos on moral grounds following a wave of concern after a Scottish scientist this year cloned a sheep.

"Cloning is the secret of eternal life. Cloning will make the life of people better by curing genetic diseases," said Rael, who like his male followers was clad in white, sporting shoulder-length hair and a moustache.
"We're not the only ones. There will be a lot of competition among laboratories offering human cloning," he told Reuters.

Rael refused to answer questions from the media about rumours of incest in the group. Nor did he reply to questions on what he did with the proceeds from Rael books, videos, pendants, watches, T-shirts, medallions, sweatshirts and hefty membership fees.
Despite Switzerland's staid international reputation, the Raelian group is not the only off-beat organisation to have made a home in these Alpine valleys and mountains.
The same mountains were home to the Solar Temple, which gained international notoriety after mass suicides and murders killed 53 of its members in two Swiss villages and a Quebec ski resort in 1994.

In 1995, 16 Solar Temple members, including several children, died in a remote French Alpine forest clearing in a macabre ritual in which most of them were drugged and had plastic bags pulled over their heads before they were shot.
In its latest issue, Rael's magazine "Apocalypse" said: "Collective suicide among Raelians? Not tomorrow."
Gerard Ramseyer, head of police and justice in the canton of Geneva, where the number of sects has jumped to more than 120 now from 80 in January, told reporters:
"The risk of collective suicide exists in this movement and we are watching them. If Rael starts talking about collective suicide, then we will consider him a danger to the population."
